sections.skill: Explain what credit reports contain, get free reports, and dispute errors

questions.prompt: Which company is one of the three nationwide credit bureaus?

choices.text: Experian
The Federal Reserve
The IRS
Visa

questions.correct_answer: Experian
questions.intro: A credit report is a record of how you have used credit: accounts, balances, payment history, and some collections. Three nationwide credit bureaus (consumer reporting agencies) keep reports: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
questions.feedback: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion are the three nationwide credit bureaus.
sources: AnnualCreditReport.com (authorized by federal law) / FTC: Consumers can get free credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion; free weekly reports have been made permanent. (https://www.annualcreditreport.com)
FTC: Credit freezes are free at each of the three nationwide credit bureaus. (https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-credit-freezes-fraud-alerts)

questions.prompt: Where can Jordan get free credit reports from all three bureaus?

choices.text: Any website that advertises "free credit score"
The bank where Jordan opened checking
The IRS website
AnnualCreditReport.com

questions.correct_answer: AnnualCreditReport.com
questions.intro: Federal law gives you free credit reports. The official site is AnnualCreditReport.com, where free reports from all three bureaus are available (weekly, under a permanent program).
questions.feedback: AnnualCreditReport.com is the official free source.

questions.prompt: Which item is generally on a credit report?

choices.text: Whether card payments were on time
Your income and salary
Your race or religion
Your bank account balances

questions.correct_answer: Whether card payments were on time
questions.intro: Credit reports show identifying information, credit accounts (cards, loans), balances, credit limits, payment history, inquiries, and certain collections. They do not include income, bank balances, race, religion, or medical details.
questions.feedback: Payment history on credit accounts is a core part of credit reports.
sources: AnnualCreditReport.com (authorized by federal law) / FTC: Consumers can get free credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion; free weekly reports have been made permanent. (https://www.annualcreditreport.com)
FTC: Credit freezes are free at each of the three nationwide credit bureaus. (https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-credit-freezes-fraud-alerts)

questions.prompt: Jordan's report lists a credit card she never opened. What should she do?

choices.text: Ignore it, since reports are always correct
Pay off the card to make it go away
Dispute it and check for identity theft
Ignore it if her score still looks fine

questions.correct_answer: Dispute it and check for identity theft
questions.intro: If a report has an error, you can dispute it with the credit bureau (and the company that reported it). The bureau generally must investigate, usually within 30 days. An account you never opened can be a sign of identity theft.
questions.feedback: Disputing errors is free; an unknown account may mean identity theft.

misconceptions.B: Pays a debt that is not hers

questions.prompt: Who may legally see Jordan's credit report?

choices.text: A lender reviewing her application
Any curious neighbor who wants to know
A classmate who asks
A social media follower

questions.correct_answer: A lender reviewing her application
questions.intro: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, only those with a "permissible purpose" can see your report: lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers (with your written permission), among others.
questions.feedback: Lenders evaluating applications have a permissible purpose.

questions.prompt: What is a credit history?

choices.text: A list of every purchase a person has made with cash
A list of a person's bank account balances
A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid
A record of a person's income each year

questions.correct_answer: A record of how a person has borrowed and repaid
questions.intro: Your credit history shows how you have handled borrowing: which accounts you have, how much you owe, and whether you paid on time.
questions.feedback: Credit history tracks borrowing and repayment.

misconceptions.B: Confuses credit history with bank balances
misconceptions.D: Credit reports do not list income

choices.text: To learn which stores a borrower likes best
To set the borrower's salary
To decide the borrower's taxes
To predict whether a borrower will repay

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether a borrower will repay
questions.intro: Past repayment behavior helps lenders estimate the risk that a borrower will not repay.
questions.feedback: Past repayment helps predict future repayment.

questions.prompt: A student with no loans or cards applies for credit. What problem might she face?

choices.text: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
Her report will show many late payments from the past
She will be approved for any amount
She has a perfect score by default

questions.correct_answer: A "thin" credit file with little history to judge
questions.intro: People with few or no credit accounts have "thin" files, which makes it harder for lenders to judge them.
questions.feedback: No history makes approval harder, not easier.

sections.skill: Reading a credit report line by line

questions.prompt: A report line shows: "Card A — limit $2,000 — balance $600 — status: 30 days late (March)". What does "30 days late" mean?

choices.text: The card was opened 30 days ago
The card has 30 days of interest-free time each month
The balance is $30
A payment was at least 30 days past due in March

questions.correct_answer: A payment was at least 30 days past due in March
questions.intro: Credit report account lines show the creditor, limit or loan amount, balance, and payment status by month. Late payments are usually reported once they are 30 or more days past due.
questions.feedback: A 30-day late payment was reported for March.

questions.prompt: A report shows two "hard inquiries" from lenders this month. What caused them?

choices.text: Applications for new credit
Checking your own report
Receiving a preapproved offer in the mail
Paying a bill on time

questions.correct_answer: Applications for new credit
questions.intro: A hard inquiry happens when a lender checks your credit because you applied for credit; it can lower scores slightly for a short time. Soft inquiries, such as checking your own report or prescreened offers, do not affect scores.
questions.feedback: Hard inquiries come from credit applications.

questions.prompt: Ana reviews her reports from all three bureaus. Why might they differ?

choices.text: One of them must be fake
Bureaus copy each other's reports exactly every day
Each bureau uses a different person's data
Not every lender reports to every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Not every lender reports to every bureau
questions.intro: Lenders choose which bureaus to report to, and reporting dates differ, so the three reports may not match exactly.
questions.feedback: Different reporting leads to differences; check all three.

misconceptions.B: Assumes the three bureaus share one file

sections.skill: Freezes, fraud alerts, and identity protection

questions.prompt: What does a credit freeze do?

choices.text: It lowers your credit score
It closes your existing cards
It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
It stops you from using your own debit card or checks

questions.correct_answer: It blocks most new lenders from seeing your report
questions.intro: A credit freeze (security freeze) restricts access to your credit report, so identity thieves cannot easily open new accounts in your name. Freezes are free at each bureau, and you can lift them temporarily when you apply for credit.
questions.feedback: A freeze blocks most new-credit checks without affecting your score or existing accounts.

misconceptions.B: Confuses freezing a report with closing accounts
misconceptions.D: Confuses a credit freeze with freezing a bank account

$100 one time
A fee of 1% of your total credit limit
Nothing; freezes are free by law

questions.correct_answer: Nothing; freezes are free by law

questions.feedback: Freezes are free at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

questions.prompt: How is a fraud alert different from a credit freeze?

choices.text: An alert closes your existing accounts
A freeze costs money; an alert is free
An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
They are identical; both close your current accounts

questions.correct_answer: An alert asks for ID checks; a freeze blocks access
questions.intro: A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity before opening credit. A credit freeze blocks most access to your report.
questions.feedback: Alerts add verification; freezes restrict access.

Sharing passwords with friends
Using the same password everywhere
